newsitem.title: IRAN: Millions of Iranians march in Shi'ite Moslem rite.
newsitem.headline: Millions of Iranians march in Shi'ite Moslem rite.

text.p: Millions of Shi'ite Moslems marched in Iran on Saturday, flailing their backs and thumping their chests to commemorate Ashoura, climax of the religion's most sorrowful period.

Processions of men, youths and boys in black shirts beating their backs with chains to the rhythm of cymbals and drums were held throughout the Islamic republic to mark the death in battle 13 centuries ago of the Prophet Mohammad's grandson Hussein.
Tehran radio said all cities and villages in the country were covered in black and immersed in gloom and mourning.
The martyrdom of Hussein at Kerbala in Iraq in 680 at the hands of troops of the Caliph Yazid established the rival Sunni branch of Islam as the religion's dominant tradition.

Shi'ites now make up only 10 percent of the world's one billion Moslems, but in Iran their faith is the state religion and its clergymen have run the country of 60 million since their revolution toppled the Shah in 1979.

Ashoura, the biggest mass event in the Shi'ite calendar, is also observed in other countries with sizeable Shi'ite communities, including Afghanistan, Bahrain, Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Syria and Saudi Arabia's oil-rich Eastern Province.
Tehran radio said Ashoura was also observed in Central Asian countries including Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Kyrgystan and Uzbekistan.
It also told listeners mourning ceremonies were held in Azerbaijan, Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, Russia, Australia, Britain and the United States.

The name Shi'ite or Shi'a meaning "a partisan" derives from the Arabic shi'at Ali -- the party of Ali, Mohammad's cousin and son-in-law who was passed over in the succession after the death of Islam's founder.
He later became Islam's fourth Caliph.
Ashoura falls on the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the lunar Islamic calendar which is observed by Shi'ites as a period of mourning.
The self-flagellation in marches through cities, towns and villages is penance for failing to come to the aid of Hussein, a Shi'ite Imam or intermediary between man and God, in his hour of need.
Some 10,000 Shi'ite clergymen were sent around the country to lead the processions.
At a working class neighbourhood in south Tehran, scores of processions converged on a shrine in a scene repeated all over the country.
Women and girls sprinkled rose-water on the marchers and queued for free handouts of food and drink.

In Tehran's teeming bazaar, shops remained shuttered for the holiday but tens of thousands jammed the streets to hear epic poems recounting Hussein's demise. Many wept as they heard of the wounds inflicted on Hussein.
Electronic synthesisers, popular in recent years, were banned during the processions as part of Iran's campaign to halt what it sees as a Western cultural invasion.
At the feverish peak of the flagellation, men used to strike their shaven heads with scimitars and daggers, sometimes producing horrific injuries.
Three years ago the Interior Ministry banned the practice.

"Wounding one's head with daggers is not in Islamic tradition...we should not do things that would make us appear as a superstitious and illogical group in the eyes of Moslems and non-Moslems in the world," Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said at the time.
Overnight, Hussein's martyrdom continued to be re-enacted in gory detail in a passion play -- Ta'aziyah -- performed in the Shi'ite world in the days leading up to the anniversary.

In Besht-e Zahra south of Tehran, at the mausoleum of the founder of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, thousands of families stayed up through the night in an atmosphere of mourning mixed with festivity to observe Ashoura.
Children clad in green representing the orphans of those slain with Hussein paraded on camels.
The anniversary is observed as a beneficent religious holiday by the dominant Sunni branch of Islam.
